I gained a bit of weight by eating a little too liberally during my last marathon training cycle, and my BMI was hovering around 23.

Calorie counting is kind of a bullshit chore, IMO - it's not that hard to just control some portions and limit my FroYo intake to below three times a week - but I decided that it might be a novel thing to generate some evidence of how easy and effective the CICO "diet" is - and also that it works.

I'm M/33/5'9" and I started out somewhere around 156-157. That was 50 days ago.

Since then, I have meticulously tracked everything I've ate. Unlike the 0-accountability fats who fail at this kind of thing, I did not, in fact, lie at all about a single thing I ate (or didn't eat). There are no fake entries and while I may have forgotten a couple of food items here and there, I've generated enough test data for long enough that a few 100-kcal slipups here and there are not enough to substantially alter the results.

My profile is totally public. My choices are godawful and I'm probably going to die any minute from malnutrition.

I synced my profile with my Garmin account, so all of my exercise data is also imported and is taken into account for the net calorie computation. Interesting to note that I also export my data to Strava, and Strava estimates the calorie consumption for the same activities as significantly higher (usually by 25% or more).

The summary of the numbers are:

  • Days: 50
  • Total in: 90,232
  • Total out: 110,346 (based on an estimated BMR of 1650kcal/day)
  • Net deficit: 20,114
  • Predicted loss: 5.75 lbs
  • Starting weight: 157
  • Weight 50 days later: 150.6
  • Actual loss: 6.4lbs

Would ya look at that? It's almost like 95% of diets don't fail. It's almost like if you have a little bit of personal fucking accountability you can effect nearly exactly the predicted loss (in my case, even more than predicted) just by consuming no more than a free website tells you to consume.

As we all know weight fluctuates quite a bit but you can see my (sort-of) daily weigh ins as a graph on MFP, and because I run and it's summer, my weight is highly sensitive to my hydration level. I can store a lot of glycogen, which requires a lot of water. It's not uncommon for me to lose as many as 5 pounds on a single run.

Also worth noting is that while I was cutting calories, I was also training for a highly rigorous 50k trail race with over a mile of elevation gain; you can see a very clear pattern of large consumption on Saturdays which are the days I burned 2000+ calories on 3, 4, and 5 hour training runs on the trails. (Sadly, I got sick with a massive chest cold the week of the race and I DNF'd at the half way point).

Anyway, I know this kind of thing has been done before but I wanted to provide personal proof that CICO works so that when my fat friends & family whine about how easy it is for me to lose weight I can just point them at MFP and say yes, yes it is easy to lose weight, just eat the way I do (well, maybe cut out the absurd amount of sugar and avoid the 3.5kcal binge days unless you're also spending 5 hours running trails) and you too will have predictable results.
We should all print it off and stick it on the face of everyone who says that CICO doesn't work

You might be running into bonk.

May have to start getting more regimented/scheduled w/ regard to time between meals as well as carb intake so you can maintain adequate levels of stored glycogen.

Your muscles need glycogen to function. Running burns through glycogen rapidly and is funneling large amounts to your running muscles at the expense of others. This will naturally cause you to feel depleted and weak when you try to post impressive powerlifting numbers. You'll also feel it if you try to do hill running at the tail end of a multi-running day sequence (e.g., if you rest Monday, do hills on Tue, flats on Wed, and then try hills on Thu, you should be able to notice a difference in your climbing compared to Tue's effort).

I run 5 days per week and I lift only 2 or 3. My running schedule is Tue/Wed/Thu/Sat/Sun. I lift on Tue/Fri and sometimes Mon but usually not. If I try to lift on Wed or Thu I always feel weak and depleted.

That said it's OK if you can't lift heavy or you can't rep out the same #. Gains come from lifting as hard as you can for as long as you can and giving your body enough protein.
